lesson.title: The -ar Engine: Verbs from Nouns
lesson.subtitle: Noun → verb: confirmación → confirmar. Hundreds of infinitives, ready to use

hook.title: Converting Nouns into Pure Action
hook.content: Every time English has a Latinate noun in -ation, Spanish has an active verb in -ar waiting for you. Confirmation becomes confirmar. Organization becomes organizar. Celebration becomes celebrar. Visitation becomes visitar. One rule hands you hundreds of first-conjugation infinitives for free!

pattern.title: Stacking Infinitives & Hooking Pronouns to the Tail
pattern.content: Spanish infinitives end in -ar and stress the final syllable: confirMAR, celeBRAR. With quiero, no extra word like English 'to' is needed: quiero confirmar ('I want to confirm'). Even better: when an infinitive is present, object pronouns can hook directly onto the tail of the infinitive as one word: quiero invitarlo ('I want to invite him/it')!
pattern.linguist_note: Latin first-conjugation -āre verbs survived robustly in Spanish. Enclitic pronouns attach to infinitives, gerunds, and affirmative commands.
pattern.trap_note: Remember to strip the whole -ación before attaching -ar: celebración → celebrar (never *celebratar!).

diagnosis.slip: wrote invitar lo as two words
diagnosis.cue: When a pronoun follows an infinitive, it welds onto the end as a single word: invitarlo.

exercises.prompt: Which English word-for-word blueprint mirrors Spanish 'Quiero invitarlo'?
exercises.meaning: I want to invite him (literal Spanish blueprint: I-want to-invite-him)
exercises.explanation: Quiero ('I-want') + invitarlo ('to-invite-him'): two Spanish words do the work of five English words!

summary.outcome: Convert -ation nouns to -ar verbs, stack them after quiero without 'to', and hook pronouns onto infinitives.

use_example.german: Quiero confirmar la reservación y quiero invitarlo.
use_example.english: I want to confirm the reservation and I want to invite him.

summary.takeaway: Spanish verbs stack without English 'to' — and pronouns can hook right onto the infinitive's tail.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([301] The Celebrar Trap): make sure you never fall into the English '-ate' ghost-syllable trap.

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'Do you want to participate, a little?'
twist.explanation: ¿Quieres participar, un poco? stacks question verb, infinitive, and qualifier.

foreshadow.line: We know how to want things and how to act; in Topic 4, we learn how to cleanly refuse them with a single word.

payoff.text: Those -ción nouns you mastered in Topic 2 now become verbs: strip -ación and attach -ar.

confirmar.etymology_derivation: confirmación → confirmar. Strip -ación, attach -ar. One rule turns hundreds of nouns into verbs.

organizar.context_translation: I want to organize the party.
organizar.etymology_derivation: organización → organizar. The infinitive in -ar is stressed on the final syllable.

celebrar.etymology_derivation: celebración → celebrar. The trap: not *celebratar. Strip the whole -ación before adding -ar.

participar.context_translation: I want to participate a little.
participar.etymology_derivation: participación → participar. Sounds everyday in Spanish, whereas 'participate' sounds formal in English.

visitar.etymology_derivation: visitation → visitar. No preposition 'to' needed in Spanish: quiero visitar (two words where English needs three).

invitar.etymology_derivation: invitación → invitar. Pronouns hook onto the infinitive: quiero invitarlo ('I want to invite him/it').

querer.etymology_derivation: Latin quaerere ('to seek, ask for') evolved in Spanish to 'to want' and 'to love'. When you make an inquiry in English, you are asking what you want.

lo.etymology_derivation: Latin illum → lo. Walks one step to the left of conjugated verbs: I it want.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).
